content.title: Integration by Parts and Partial Fractions
content.overview: This lesson focuses on two advanced integration techniques: Integration by Parts (IBP), which reverses the product rule, and Partial Fraction Decomposition, which simplifies proper rational functions into integrable terms. Mastery involves identifying the correct structure of the integrand and executing multi-step algebraic and calculus procedures accurately.
learning_objectives: Identify when to apply integration by parts versus partial fraction decomposition.
Apply the integration by parts formula to evaluate integrals of products.
Decompose proper rational functions into simpler fractions for integration.
Evaluate definite integrals using these techniques while maintaining accuracy with constants and limits.

sections.title: Integration by Parts (IBP)
sections.content: Integration by parts is used when the integrand is a product of two functions, typically where one function simplifies when differentiated and the other is easily integrated. The formula is derived from the product rule: ∫ u dv = uv - ∫ v du. A common strategy for choosing 'u' is the LIATE mnemonic (Logarithmic, Inverse trigonometric, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential), where functions appearing earlier in the list are better candidates for 'u'. For a definite integral from a to b, the formula is [uv]_a^b - ∫_a^b v du.

sections.title: Partial Fraction Decomposition
sections.content: This technique is applied to proper rational functions—functions where the degree of the numerator is strictly less than the degree of the denominator. If the denominator can be factored into distinct linear factors, such as (x - r)(x - s), the fraction can be rewritten as A/(x - r) + B/(x - s). To find the constants A and B, multiply the entire equation by the common denominator and solve the resulting identity by substituting convenient x-values or equating coefficients. Once decomposed, these terms integrate into natural logarithm functions.

sections.title: Strategic Selection and Execution
sections.content:
Success in AP Calculus BC requires rapid classification. If you see a polynomial multiplied by a transcendental function (like x*sin(x)), use IBP. If you see a fraction with a factorable polynomial denominator, use Partial Fractions. Always verify that a rational function is 'proper' before decomposing; if the numerator's degree is equal to or greater than the denominator's, you must perform polynomial long division first.

![A flow chart showing the decision process between Integration by Parts and Partial Fractions.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/241b0581-ff8f-41c6-b57d-4915da4cf3ba-1786519366933-42.webp)

worked_examples.question: Evaluate the definite integral I = ∫_0^1 [x * e^(2x) + (7x + 5)/(x^2 + 3x + 2)] dx.
worked_examples.solution:
Step 1: Split the integral into two parts. Part A is a product (IBP); Part B is a rational function (Partial Fractions).

Step 2 (Part A): Let u = x and dv = e^(2x) dx. Then du = dx and v = (1/2)e^(2x). 
Using ∫ u dv = uv - ∫ v du: 
[(1/2)x * e^(2x)]_0^1 - ∫_0^1 (1/2)e^(2x) dx 
= [(1/2)(1)e^2 - 0] - [(1/4)e^(2x)]_0^1 
= (1/2)e^2 - [(1/4)e^2 - 1/4] 
= (1/4)e^2 + 1/4.

Step 3 (Part B): Factor the denominator: x^2 + 3x + 2 = (x + 1)(x + 2). 
Set up decomposition: (7x + 5)/((x + 1)(x + 2)) = A/(x + 1) + B/(x + 2). 
Multiply by denominator: 7x + 5 = A(x + 2) + B(x + 1). 
If x = -1: -7 + 5 = A(1) => A = -2. 
If x = -2: -14 + 5 = B(-1) => B = 9. 
Integrate: ∫_0^1 [-2/(x + 1) + 9/(x + 2)] dx = [-2 ln|x + 1| + 9 ln|x + 2|]_0^1 
= (-2 ln 2 + 9 ln 3) - (-2 ln 1 + 9 ln 2) 
= 9 ln 3 - 11 ln 2.

Step 4: Combine results. I = (e^2 + 1)/4 + 9 ln 3 - 11 ln 2.

common_mistakes: Forgetting the 'minus' sign in the IBP formula: ∫ u dv = uv - ∫ v du.
Failing to distribute the negative sign when evaluating the second part of the IBP formula over a definite interval.
Attempting partial fraction decomposition on an improper fraction without performing long division first.
Incorrectly integrating 1/(ax+b) by forgetting the 1/a constant (e.g., integrating 1/(2x+1) as ln|2x+1| instead of 1/2 ln|2x+1|).
exam_tips: Use the 'Heaviside Cover-up Method' for quick partial fraction constants when dealing with non-repeated linear factors.
When using IBP, if 'u' is a polynomial of degree n, you will likely need to apply the process n times, or use the tabular method.
Always check if a simple u-substitution works before jumping to IBP or Partial Fractions; it is faster and less prone to error.
In the free-response section, show the setup of your A and B equations to earn partial credit even if your arithmetic fails.
content.recap: Integration by parts reverses the product rule using the formula ∫ u dv = uv - ∫ v du. Partial fraction decomposition breaks down proper rational functions into simpler, integrable logarithmic terms. Both require careful management of algebraic signs and constants during definite integration.

knowledge_claims.content: The integration by parts formula is defined as the integral of u dv equals uv minus the integral of v du.
To apply integration by parts to a definite integral from a to b, evaluate the term [uv] from a to b and subtract the definite integral of v du from a to b.
Partial fraction decomposition can only be directly applied to proper rational functions where the degree of the numerator is less than the degree of the denominator.
If a rational function is improper, polynomial long division must be performed to obtain a polynomial plus a proper rational remainder before decomposing.
An integrand consisting of a product of an algebraic function and a transcendental function (like x*cos(x)) is a primary signal for using integration by parts.
A rational function with a factorable quadratic or higher-degree denominator is a primary signal for using partial fraction decomposition.
The constants A and B in a linear partial fraction decomposition represent the numerators that, when summed over their respective factors, reconstruct the original numerator.
A common error in integration by parts is failing to correctly identify 'dv' as a term that includes the 'dx' differential.
After performing partial fraction decomposition, the result can be verified by finding a common denominator for the new fractions and checking if the resulting numerator matches the original.
Integrating a term like A/(x + r) results in A * ln|x + r| + C, assuming the coefficient of x is 1.
Integration by parts is the integral calculus equivalent of the differential calculus product rule.
When solving for constants in partial fractions, substituting the roots of the denominator into the equation is an efficient method to isolate and solve for each constant.

items.stem: Which procedure or value is mathematically consistent in “AP Calculus BC — Integration by Parts and Partial Fractions — Practice Record 01”?

options.A: Integration by Parts and Partial Fractions: Integration by parts reverses the product rule, while partial fractions decomposes rational functions into simpler integrable terms.
options.B: Average Value and Net Change: The average value of a function divides its integral by interval length, while net change integrates a rate with signs preserved.
options.C: Arc Length of Parametric and Vector Curves: Arc length accumulates speed, using the square root of the sum of squared component derivatives.
options.D: Alternating Series and Error: An alternating series converges when magnitudes decrease to zero, and its truncation error is bounded by the first omitted magnitude.

items.explanation: Choice A is best because Integration by parts reverses the product rule, while partial fractions decomposes rational functions into simpler integrable terms. The other options invoke different atomic topics and do not satisfy the record's stated target as directly.

items.stem: Which relationship connects the verbal and symbolic information in “AP Calculus BC — Integration by Parts and Partial Fractions — Practice Record 02”?

options.A: Area Between Curves: Area between curves integrates top minus bottom or right minus left after locating relevant intersections and interval changes.
options.B: Integration by Parts and Partial Fractions: Integration by parts reverses the product rule, while partial fractions decomposes rational functions into simpler integrable terms.
options.C: Polar Coordinates and Derivatives: Polar points use radius and angle, and polar slope follows from parametric differentiation of x=r cos theta and y=r sin theta.
options.D: Ratio and Root Tests: Ratio and root limits below one imply absolute convergence and above one imply divergence, while a limit of one is inconclusive.
